claim: Mitochondria undergo cycles of fission and fusion at a unified platform defined by ER-mitochondria membrane contact sites (MCSs).
source: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles that undergo cycles of fission and fusion at a unified platform defined by endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-mitochondria membrane contact sites (MCSs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: ER-mitochondria MCSs co-localize fission and fusion machinery.
source: These MCSs or nodes co-localize fission and fusion machinery.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as an established observation.

claim: ABHD16A is a major regulator of ER-associated mitochondrial node formation.
source: We have used a promiscuous biotin ligase linked to the fusion machinery, Mfn1, and proteomics to identify an ER membrane protein, ABHD16A, as a major regulator of node formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on proximity proteomics experiments.

claim: In the absence of ABHD16A, fission and fusion machineries fail to recruit to ER-associated mitochondrial nodes.
source: In the absence of ABHD16A, fission and fusion machineries fail to recruit to ER-associated mitochondrial nodes, and fission and fusion rates are significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Fission and fusion rates are significantly reduced in the absence of ABHD16A.
source: In the absence of ABHD16A, fission and fusion machineries fail to recruit to ER-associated mitochondrial nodes, and fission and fusion rates are significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: ABHD16A contains an acyltransferase motif and an α/β hydrolase domain.
source: ABHD16A contains an acyltransferase motif and an α/β hydrolase domain, and point mutations in critical residues of these regions fail to rescue the formation of ER-associated mitochondrial hot spots.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by domain analysis.

claim: Point mutations in critical residues of the acyltransferase motif and α/β hydrolase domain fail to rescue the formation of ER-associated mitochondrial hot spots.
source: ABHD16A contains an acyltransferase motif and an α/β hydrolase domain, and point mutations in critical residues of these regions fail to rescue the formation of ER-associated mitochondrial hot spots.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from mutagenesis studies.

claim: ABHD16A functions by altering phospholipid composition at ER-mitochondria MCSs.
source: These data suggest a mechanism whereby ABHD16A functions by altering phospholipid composition at ER-mitochondria MCSs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the domain structure and mutational analysis.

claim: ABHD16A is the first example of an ER membrane protein that regulates the recruitment of both fission and fusion machineries to mitochondria.
source: Our data present the first example of an ER membrane protein that regulates the recruitment of both fission and fusion machineries to mitochondria.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Mitochondria maintain their overall architecture and morphology by undergoing cycles of fission and fusion.
source: Mitochondria maintain their overall architecture and morphology by undergoing cycles of fission and fusion (Friedman et al., 2010; Twig et al., 2008; Youle and van der Bliek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of fission and fusion cycles results in fragmentation or elongation, which can be detrimental to cell health and is associated with various disease states.
source: Disruption of these cycles results in fragmentation or elongation, which can be detrimental to cell health and is associated with various disease states (Rambold et al., 2011; Wai and Langer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both fission and fusion processes are first initiated by the ER at ER-mitochondria membrane contact sites.
source: Both processes are first initiated by the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) at ER-mitochondria membrane contact sites (MCSs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: INF2 and Spire1c are actin nucleators linked to ER-associated mitochondrial fission.
source: Several factors have been linked to ER-associated mitochondrial fission, including two actin nucleators, INF2 and Spire1c, which are proposed to polymerize actin at ER-mitochondria MCSs to initiate constriction of the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM; Korobova et al., 2013; Manor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: INF2 and Spire1c polymerize actin at ER-mitochondria MCSs to initiate constriction of the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Several factors have been linked to ER-associated mitochondrial fission, including two actin nucleators, INF2 and Spire1c, which are proposed to polymerize actin at ER-mitochondria MCSs to initiate constriction of the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM; Korobova et al., 2013; Manor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Drp1 and Dyn2 are GTPases recruited to the OMM at ER MCSs to further constrict the OMM, leading to mitochondrial division.
source: Subsequently, two GTPases (Drp1 and Dyn2) are recruited to the OMM at ER MCSs to further constrict the OMM, which leads to mitochondrial division (Bleazard et al., 1999; Ferguson and De Camilli, 2012; Labrousse et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2016; Smirnova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ER-mitochondria MCSs dictate sites where OMM fusion occurs via Mfn1/2 oligomerization in trans to drive membrane fusion upon GTP hydrolysis.
source: ER-mitochondria MCSs also dictate sites where OMM fusion occurs via Mfn1/2 oligomerization in trans to drive membrane fusion upon GTP hydrolysis (Abrisch et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2003; Guo et al., 2018; Santel and Fuller, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inner mitochondrial membrane fusion occurs via the GTPase Opa1.
source: Subsequently, inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) fusion occurs via the GTPase, Opa1 (Ban et al., 2017; Herlan et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2004; Legros et al., 2002; Meeusen et al., 2006; Misaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cycles of fission and fusion occur at the same location or hot spots that are spatially dictated by the ER.
source: We have recently discovered that cycles of fission and fusion occur at the same location or hot spots that are spatially dictated by the ER.
evidence: This is a recent finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Predefined branch points, or nodes, are where both fission (Drp1) and fusion (Mfn1) machineries converge.
source: These predefined branch points, or nodes, are where both fission (Drp1) and fusion (Mfn1) machineries converge (Abrisch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TurboID can biotinylate proteins within a ~10–30 nm range upon biotin addition.
source: TurboID can biotinylate proteins within a ~10–30 nm range upon the addition of biotin (Branon et al., 2018; Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing TurboID.

claim: V5-TurboID-Mfn1 co-localized well with GFP-Mfn1 puncta on mitochondria in HeLa cells.
source: By immunofluorescence, V5-TurboID-Mfn1 (magenta, with V5 antibody) co-localized well with GFP-Mfn1 (green) puncta on mitochondria (mito-BFP, blue) in HeLa cells (Figure 1B, top panels).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mfn1E209A mutant is deficient in its ability to hydrolyze GTP, does not homodimerize, and cannot drive fusion.
source: This mutant is deficient in its ability to hydrolyze GTP, does not homodimerize, cannot drive fusion (Cao et al., 2017; Sloat et al., 2019), and does not enrich at ER-mitochondria MCSs with wild type (WT) GFP-Mfn1 puncta (compare magenta to green, Figure 1B, bottom panels) consistent with previous reports (Abrisch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mfn1E209A does not enrich at ER-mitochondria MCSs with wild type GFP-Mfn1 puncta.
source: This mutant is deficient in its ability to hydrolyze GTP, does not homodimerize, cannot drive fusion (Cao et al., 2017; Sloat et al., 2019), and does not enrich at ER-mitochondria MCSs with wild type (WT) GFP-Mfn1 puncta (compare magenta to green, Figure 1B, bottom panels) consistent with previous reports (Abrisch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations.

claim: ABHD16A is reported to be a phospholipid hydrolase with the highest affinity for phosphatidylserine lipolysis.
source: ABHD16A is reported to be a phospholipid hydrolase, with the highest affinity for phosphotidylserine (PS) lipolysis that resides on the ER membrane via two transmembrane domains (TMDs; Kamat et al., 2015; Lord et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ABHD16A resides on the ER membrane via two transmembrane domains.
source: ABHD16A is reported to be a phospholipid hydrolase, with the highest affinity for phosphotidylserine (PS) lipolysis that resides on the ER membrane via two transmembrane domains (TMDs; Kamat et al., 2015; Lord et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ABHD16A is highly conserved in vertebrates (96% conserved from human to mouse).
source: It is highly conserved in vertebrates (96% conserved from human to mouse) and contains an alpha/beta hydrolase domain responsible for its phospholipid hydrolase activity, a predicted acyltransferase motif (H189/D194), and two predicted lipase-like motifs (GXSXXG with serines at positions S176 and S306), all of which face the cytoplasm (Figure 1H; Kamat et al., 2015; Lord et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis and supported by citations.

claim: ABHD16A contains an alpha/beta hydrolase domain responsible for its phospholipid hydrolase activity.
source: It is highly conserved in vertebrates (96% conserved from human to mouse) and contains an alpha/beta hydrolase domain responsible for its phospholipid hydrolase activity, a predicted acyltransferase motif (H189/D194), and two predicted lipase-like motifs (GXSXXG with serines at positions S176 and S306), all of which face the cytoplasm (Figure 1H; Kamat et al., 2015; Lord et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At low expression levels, ABHD16A-mNG co-localized homogenously along the ER membrane and to a much lesser degree on mitochondria.
source: At low expression levels, ABHD16A-mNG co-localized homogenously along the ER membrane (blue arrow) and to a much lesser degree on mitochondria (magenta arrow) but did not appear to accumulate at MCSs (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ABHD16A did not appear to accumulate at MCSs at low expression levels.
source: At low expression levels, ABHD16A-mNG co-localized homogenously along the ER membrane (blue arrow) and to a much lesser degree on mitochondria (magenta arrow) but did not appear to accumulate at MCSs (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Endogenous ABHD16A can be found in the MAM similar to other ER proteins and to a lesser extent in the pure mitochondrial fraction.
source: Endogenous ABHD16A localization was also analyzed by immunoblot of pure, crude, and mitochondrial-associated membrane (MAM) fractions isolated from U-2 OS cells. These data showed that endogenous ABHD16A can be found in the MAM similar to other ER proteins and to a lesser extent in the pure mitochondrial fraction, as previously reported (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Singh et al., 2020; Wieckowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and supported by citations.

claim: ABHD16A depletion significantly reduced Mfn1 puncta compared to siCTRL-treated cells.
source: ABHD16A depletion significantly reduced Mfn1 puncta compared to siCTRL-treated cells (Figure 2A and D: ~0.1 vs. 0.3 puncta per µm of mitochondria, respectively).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: Mfn1 puncta were restored by re-expression of an siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo construct.
source: Mfn1 puncta were restored by re-expression of an siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo construct (Figure 2A and D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: ABHD16A regulates localization of Mfn1 to ER-mitochondria contact sites.
source: These data demonstrate that ABHD16A regulates localization of Mfn1 to ER-mitochondria contact sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Mfn1 recruitment.

claim: Drp1 recruitment to crossings was significantly reduced in ABHD16A-depleted vs. siCTRL-treated cells (18% vs. 47%, respectively).
source: Drp1 recruitment to crossings was significantly reduced in ABHD16A-depleted vs. siCTRL-treated cells (18% vs. 47%, respectively, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 2E.

claim: The recruitment of Drp1 to ER-associated puncta could be restored by reintroduction of an siRNA-resistant ABHD16A expression construct.
source: The recruitment of Drp1 to ER-associated puncta could be restored by reintroduction of an siRNA-resistant ABHD16A expression construct (ABHD16A-Halo; Figure 2B and E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2B and quantified in Figure 2E.

claim: ABHD16A is required for Drp1 fission machinery recruitment to ER-mitochondria MCSs.
source: These data reveal that ABHD16A is also required for Drp1 fission machinery recruitment to ER-mitochondria MCSs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Drp1 recruitment.

claim: ABHD16A-depleted cells had significantly fewer nodes than control cells (~0.13 vs.~0.34 puncta per µm of mitochondria).
source: ABHD16A-depleted cells had significantly fewer nodes than control cells (~0.13 vs.~0.34 puncta per µm of mitochondria, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 2F.

claim: Mitochondrial node formation could be rescued by re-expression of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo but not the empty vector control.
source: Mitochondrial node formation could be rescued by re-expression of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo but not the empty vector (EV) control (Figure 2C and F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2F.

claim: ABHD16A is required for the co-localization of fission and fusion machineries to mitochondrial nodes.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that ABHD16A is required for the co-localization of fission and fusion machineries to mitochondrial nodes, suggesting a common mechanism is required for their recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on node formation.

claim: Fusion rates were significantly reduced in ABHD16A-depleted cells from a rate of 0.25 (siCTRL) to 0.06 (siABHD16A) fusion events per mitochondrion/minute.
source: Fusion rates were significantly reduced in ABHD16A-depleted cells (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 3—video 1, Figure 3—video 2 from a rate of 0.25 [siCTRL] to 0.06 [siABHD16A] fusion events per mitochondrion/minute).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 3D.

claim: Fusion rates could be rescued by reintroduction of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo to depleted cells.
source: Fusion rates could be rescued by reintroduction of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo to depleted cells (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 3—video 3).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 3C and quantified in Figure 3D.

claim: In siCTRL cells, the majority of fusion events occur by tip-to-middle fusion (63 out of 85 fusion events, 74% of total fusion events).
source: In siCTRL cells, the majority of events occur by tip-to-middle fusion (63 out of 85 fusion events, 74% of total fusion events, 0.19 out of 0.25 fusion events per mitochondrion/min, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 3F.

claim: Upon ABHD16A depletion, tip-to-middle fusion events are highly reduced (0.19 in siCTRL vs. 0.02 tip-to-middle fusion events per mitochondrion/min in ABHD16A depletion).
source: Upon ABHD16A depletion, tip-to-middle fusion events are highly reduced (0.19 in siCTRL vs. 0.02 tip-to-middle fusion events per mitochondrion/min in ABHD16A depletion), whereas tip-to-tip fusion is less affected (0.06 in siCTRL vs. 0.04 tip-to-tip fusion events per mitochondrion/min in ABHD16A depletion, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 3F.

claim: Tip-to-tip fusion is less affected by ABHD16A depletion (0.06 in siCTRL vs. 0.04 tip-to-tip fusion events per mitochondrion/min in ABHD16A depletion).
source: Upon ABHD16A depletion, tip-to-middle fusion events are highly reduced (0.19 in siCTRL vs. 0.02 tip-to-middle fusion events per mitochondrion/min in ABHD16A depletion), whereas tip-to-tip fusion is less affected (0.06 in siCTRL vs. 0.04 tip-to-tip fusion events per mitochondrion/min in ABHD16A depletion, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 3F.

claim: The 'middle' part of the tip-to-middle fusion event occurs at ER-associated mitochondrial constriction sites where fission and fusion machineries also assemble and co-localize.
source: What makes these results notable is that the 'middle' part of the tip-to-middle fusion event occurs at ER-associated mitochondrial constriction sites where fission and fusion machineries also assemble and co-localize (Abrisch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated based on previous work cited.

claim: Fission rates were significantly reduced upon ABHD16A depletion (a > threefold reduction from 0.17 to 0.05 fission events per mitochondrion/min).
source: Indeed, fission rates were also significantly reduced upon ABHD16A depletion (a > threefold reduction from 0.17 to 0.05 fission events per mitochondrion/min; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 3E.

claim: Fission rates could be restored by expressing exogenous siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo and not with an EV control.
source: Fission rates could also be restored by expressing exogenous siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-Halo and not with an EV control (Halo-N1; Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ABHD16A depletion reduces fusion and fission rates concomitant with the reduced recruitment of fusion and fission machineries to ER-associated nodes.
source: These data show that ABHD16A depletion reduces fusion and fission rates concomitant with the reduced recruitment of fusion and fission machineries to ER-associated nodes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on fusion and fission rates.

claim: ABHD16A is a regulator of ER-associated mitochondrial fission and fusion dynamics.
source: Taken together, ABHD16A is a regulator of ER-associated mitochondrial fission and fusion dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: ABHD16A-depleted cells had highly elongated mitochondria compared to control (4.4 µm2 vs. 2.2 µm2, respectively).
source: On average, ABHD16A-depleted cells had highly elongated mitochondria compared to control (4.4 µm2 vs. 2.2 µm2, respectively, Figure 4B, D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: Morphology could be restored to siCTRL lengths by re-expressing siRNA-resistant ABHD16A.
source: Morphology could be restored to siCTRL lengths by re-expressing siRNA-resistant ABHD16A (ABHD16A-mNG; Figure 4C and D; also see immunoblot in Figure 4E for relative expression levels).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: The depletion of ABHD16A caused mitochondrial elongation in HeLa cells, showing that this effect is not cell-type specific.
source: The depletion of ABHD16A also caused mitochondrial elongation (compared to control) in HeLa cells, showing that this effect is not cell-type specific (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–1E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-1E.

claim: ABHD16A KO U-2 OS cells display an elongated mitochondrial morphology and reduced Drp1 recruitment.
source: Consistently, ABHD16A KO U-2 OS cells also display an elongated mitochondrial morphology and reduced Drp1 recruitment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and 1G.

claim: Only re-expression of the siRNA-resistant ER-localized ABHD16A (ABHD16AER) rescues mitochondrial morphology, while rescue with the mitochondria-localized version (ABHD16Amito) does not.
source: However, only re-expression of the siRNA-resistant ER-localized ABHD16A (ABHD16AER) rescues mitochondrial morphology, while rescue with the mitochondria-localized version (ABHD16Amito) does not (Figure 4C-E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4C and quantified in Figure 4D.

claim: ABHD16A OE cells had a 3.6-fold reduction in area per mitochondrion.
source: On average, ABHD16A OE cells had a 3.6-fold reduction in area per mitochondrion (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 4G.

claim: Only the ER-localized ABHD16A (ABHD16AER) drove mitochondrial fragmentation, whereas the mitochondrial-localized form (ABHD16Amito) did not.
source: Consistent with rescue data above (Figure 4B–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), only the ER-localized ABHD16A (ABHD16AER) drove mitochondrial fragmentation, whereas the mitochondrial-localized form (ABHD16Amito) did not (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 4F and quantified in Figure 4G.

claim: The ER-localized ABHD16A regulates mitochondrial morphology from the ER.
source: Together, the depletion and OE experiments suggest that the ER-localized ABHD16A regulates mitochondrial morphology from the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on localization and morphology.

claim: ABHD16A depletion leads to 2.1-fold increase in ER-mitochondria MCS area (ddFP) compared to siCTRL-treated cells.
source: Thus, ABHD16A depletion leads to 2.1-fold increase in ER-mitochondria MCS area (ddFP) compared to siCTRL-treated cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 5D.

claim: This increased contact was reduced by re-expression of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A.
source: This increased contact was reduced by re-expression of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A (Figure 5B and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 5B and quantified in Figure 5D.

claim: ABHD16A is not an ER-mitochondria contact site tether.
source: These data suggest that ABHD16A is not an ER-mitochondria contact site tether.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ddFP contact site data.

claim: ABHD16A-depleted cells had threefold fewer ER-associated mitochondrial constrictions than siCTRL-treated cells (23 vs. 63%, respectively).
source: ABHD16A-depleted cells had threefold fewer ER-associated mitochondrial constrictions than siCTRL-treated cells (23 vs. 63%, respectively, Figure 6A and C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding quantified in Figure 6C.

claim: Re-expression of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-mNG restored levels of ER-associated mitochondrial constrictions to 75% whereas an EV control did not.
source: Re-expression of siRNA-resistant ABHD16A-mNG restored levels of ER-associated mitochondrial constrictions to 75% whereas an EV control (mNG-N1) did not (Figure 6A and C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6A and quantified in Figure 6C.

claim: ABHD16A is required for ER-associated mitochondrial membrane constriction.
source: These data reveal that ABHD16A is required for ER-associated mitochondrial membrane constriction, which explains why its depletion disrupts fission/fusion machinery recruitment and node formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on constrictions.

claim: The acyltransferase motif mutant could rescue ER-associated mitochondrial constriction to a level similar to WT rescue levels, whereas the alpha/beta hydrolase domain mutant could not.
source: The acyltransferase motif mutant could rescue ER-associated mitochondrial constriction to a level similar to WT rescue levels, whereas the alpha/beta hydrolase domain mutant could not (Figure 6A and C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6A and quantified in Figure 6C.

claim: Phospholipid hydrolysis from a dual-chain phospholipid to a single-chain phospholipid could be why ABHD16A drives ER-associated mitochondrial constriction.
source: These data suggest that phospholipid hydrolysis from a dual-chain phospholipid to a single-chain phospholipid could be why ABHD16A drives ER-associated mitochondrial constriction.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the mutational analysis.

claim: Only WT ABHD16A could restore Drp1 recruitment to ER crossings.
source: Interestingly, only WT ABHD16A could restore Drp1 recruitment to ER crossings (Figures 2B, E, 6D and F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6D and quantified in Figure 6F.

claim: Neither the acyltransferase motif nor alpha/beta hydrolase domain mutants could rescue Drp1 recruitment in ABHD16A-depleted cells.
source: Neither the acyltransferase motif nor alpha/beta hydrolase domain mutants could rescue Drp1 recruitment in ABHD16A-depleted cells (Figure 6D and F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6D and quantified in Figure 6F.

claim: Only the WT protein could restore Mfn1 accumulation at ER-mitochondria MCSs in ABHD16A-depleted cells.
source: Similar to what was seen for Drp1, only the WT protein could restore Mfn1 accumulation at ER-mitochondria MCSs in ABHD16A-depleted cells (Figures 2A, D, 6E and G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6E and quantified in Figure 6G.

claim: Both acyltransferase and alpha/beta hydrolase activities are required for the recruitment of fission and fusion machinery to ER-associated nodes.
source: Thus, both acyltransferase and alpha/beta hydrolase activities are required for the recruitment of fission and fusion machinery to ER-associated nodes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis.

claim: Only the WT ABHD16A can rescue overall mitochondrial morphology.
source: Consistent with these results, only the WT ABHD16A can rescue overall mitochondrial morphology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F and quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Mutating the predicted catalytic serines of both lipase-like motifs (S176A and S306A) could still rescue mitochondrial morphology similarly to WT ABHD16A.
source: However, we have determined that mutating the predicted catalytic serines of both motifs (S176A and S306A) could still rescue mitochondrial morphology similarly to WT ABHD16A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F and quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The lipase-like motifs have either no function or no role in regulating mitochondrial dynamics.
source: We therefore concluded that these lipase-like motifs have either no function or no role in regulating mitochondrial dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis of lipase-like motifs.

claim: While the alpha/beta hydrolase domain is sufficient for ER-associated mitochondrial constriction, the acyltransferase motif is still required to form active nodes for fission and fusion.
source: So, while the alpha/beta hydrolase domain is sufficient for ER-associated mitochondrial constriction, the acyltransferase motif is still required to form active nodes for fission and fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis.

claim: The mechanism of ER-associated mitochondrial node formation is a multistep process that requires several modifications of phospholipids.
source: These data suggest that the mechanism of ER-associated mitochondrial node formation is a multistep process that requires several modifications of phospholipids.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the requirement for both motifs.

claim: ORP8 has been proposed to transfer phospholipids, such as PS, to other organelles at ER-mitochondria and ER-PM MCSs.
source: Two published ER-localized lipid transfer proteins were worthy candidates: ORP8, which has been proposed to transfer phospholipids, such as PS, to other organelles at ER-mitochondria and ER-PM MCSs (Chung et al., 2015; Galmes et al., 2016) and the VPS13A/VPS13D paralogs, which have demonstrated roles in facilitating lipid transfer between the ER and other organelles at MCSs (Guillén-Samander et al., 2021a; Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VPS13A/VPS13D paralogs have demonstrated roles in facilitating lipid transfer between the ER and other organelles at MCSs.
source: Two published ER-localized lipid transfer proteins were worthy candidates: ORP8, which has been proposed to transfer phospholipids, such as PS, to other organelles at ER-mitochondria and ER-PM MCSs (Chung et al., 2015; Galmes et al., 2016) and the VPS13A/VPS13D paralogs, which have demonstrated roles in facilitating lipid transfer between the ER and other organelles at MCSs (Guillén-Samander et al., 2021a; Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neither ORP8 depletion nor VPS13A/13D depletion by siRNA treatment altered mitochondrial morphology compared to siCTRL-treated cells.
source: Neither ORP8 depletion nor VPS13A/13D depletion by siRNA treatment altered mitochondrial morphology compared to siCTRL-treated cells (Figure 7A, C, D and E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7A and 7C and quantified in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: ABHD16A-mCh OE promotes mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: ABHD16A-mCh OE promotes mitochondrial fragmentation as previously described (Figures 4F, 7B and C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: Mitochondrial morphology is dramatically rescued upon ORP8 depletion and re-fragmented by exogenous siRNA-resistant ORP8 re-expression in the ABHD16AOE/ORP8-depleted cells.
source: However, mitochondrial morphology is dramatically rescued upon ORP8 depletion and re-fragmented by exogenous siRNA-resistant ORP8 re-expression in the ABHD16AOE/ORP8-depleted cells (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7B and quantified in Figure 7D.

claim: Depletion of both VPS13A and VPS13D did not prevent ABHD16A OE-induced fragmentation.
source: In contrast, depletion of both VPS13A and VPS13D did not prevent ABHD16A OE-induced fragmentation (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding shown in Figure 7C and quantified in Figure 7E.

claim: ORP8, but not VPS13A/D, facilitates ABHD16A activity during ER-associated mitochondrial constriction.

claim: ABHD16A could promote membrane curvature for mitochondrial fission and fusion through modifying the SN2 position of phospholipids to increase acyl chain asymmetry.
source: Alternatively, several acyltransferase proteins can modify the SN2 position of phospholipids to increase acyl chain asymmetry to potentiate membrane bending and curvature (Harayama et al., 2014; Hishikawa et al., 2014; Hofmann, 2000; Manni et al., 2018; Shindou et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2008). Through this mechanism, ABHD16A could promote membrane curvature for mitochondrial fission and fusion.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

source: More specifically, in yeast, the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES) complex, which is proposed to transfer ER PS and PC to mitochondrial membranes, (Jeong et al., 2017; Kojima et al., 2016; Kornmann et al., 2009) assembles between the ER and mitochondrial membranes at MCSs (Michel and Kornmann, 2012; Murley et al., 2013).
